title: Relational (SQL) vs NoSQL stores
summary: Decide whether your data and access patterns suit a relational database or a non-relational store such as key-value, document or wide-column.

values.sql: Tables with a fixed schema and relationships between them
values.nosql: Flexible records addressed by key or document, often denormalised

values.sql: Rich ad-hoc queries, joins and aggregations
values.nosql: Fast by key or a few predefined access patterns; joins are limited or absent
Often single-item atomicity; multi-item transactions vary by product

values.sql: Scales up easily; scaling out needs sharding work
values.nosql: Designed to scale out horizontally by partition key

values.sql: Strong consistency on a single primary
values.nosql: Often tunable, with eventual consistency as a common default

values.sql: Explicit migrations, safer but slower to change
values.nosql: Flexible, but the application must handle varying shapes

sql: Data is relational and queried in many ways you cannot predict yet.
You need multi-row transactions, for example payments or inventory.
The dataset fits comfortably on one primary with replicas.
nosql: Access is mostly by key and the patterns are known in advance.
You need very high write throughput or horizontal scale from the start.
Records are self-contained documents or time-ordered events.

watchOut: Choosing NoSQL for scale you do not have, then re-implementing joins in application code.
Treating SQL as unable to scale: read replicas and careful indexing go a long way before sharding.

title: Message queue vs event stream (log)
summary: Choose between a broker that delivers and deletes messages and a replicated log that keeps events for replay.

values.queue: Broker routes a message to a consumer, which acknowledges it and the message is removed
values.stream: Append-only partitioned log that consumers read at their own offset

values.queue: Not possible once a message is acknowledged
values.stream: Consumers can rewind and reprocess history while retained

values.queue: Competing consumers share work on one queue
values.stream: Many independent consumer groups each read the full stream

values.queue: Best effort, or strict only in FIFO variants with limits
values.stream: Ordered within a partition; choose the key to group related events

values.queue: Good for task distribution at moderate rates
values.stream: Built for very high throughput through sequential writes and partitioning

values.queue: Background jobs, task distribution, per-message routing
values.stream: Event pipelines, analytics, change data capture, multiple readers of the same data

queue: You distribute jobs where each message is handled once by one worker.
You need flexible routing, priorities or per-message delay.
You do not need to keep or replay old messages.
stream: Several systems need the same events independently.
You need replay to rebuild state or recover from a bug.
Volume is high and ordering per key matters.

watchOut: Assuming exactly-once delivery: design consumers to be idempotent either way.
Using a stream as a task queue and fighting its partition and offset semantics.

title: Replication: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless
summary: Pick how copies of data stay in sync, trading write availability against the complexity of conflicts.

values.multi: Several leaders, often one per region
values.leaderless: Any replica, with the client or a coordinator writing to several

values.leader: None: one writer defines the order
values.multi: Concurrent writes conflict and need resolution
values.leaderless: Possible; resolved by versioning or last write wins

values.leader: Needs leader election and can cause brief write unavailability
values.leaderless: No failover step; quorums tolerate node loss

values.leader: Followers can lag; read from the leader for the latest data
values.multi: Reads in one region may be behind another
values.leaderless: Tunable with quorum sizes (R + W greater than N)

leader: Most applications: simple reasoning and strong consistency for writes.
Reads dominate and followers can absorb them.
multi: Users in several regions need low-latency local writes.
You can define a sound conflict-resolution rule.
leaderless: You need very high write availability and tolerate eventual consistency.
You are building or using a Dynamo-style store.

watchOut: Reading from a lagging follower right after a write: route those reads to the leader or use read-your-writes.
Last write wins silently discards one of two concurrent updates.

title: Sharding: range, hash or directory
summary: Choose how records are assigned to shards, balancing even load against efficient range queries.

rows.dimension: How a key maps to a shard

values.hash: Hash of the key modulo or on a ring
values.directory: A lookup table maps each key or tenant to a shard
Depends on how entries are assigned

values.range: Risk of hot ranges, for example the newest timestamps
values.directory: Fully controllable, including moving hot tenants

values.hash: Consistent hashing moves only a fraction of keys; plain modulo reshuffles most
values.directory: Update the directory and move the chosen data
The directory itself must be fast and highly available

range: Queries scan ordered ranges, such as time series.
You can manage hot ranges, for example by salting keys.
hash: Access is mostly by key and even distribution matters most.
You expect to add nodes and want minimal data movement (use consistent hashing).
directory: You shard by tenant with very uneven sizes.
You need to move specific data between shards deliberately.

watchOut: A shard key that does not match your queries forces cross-shard scans.
Hash modulo N moves almost every key when N changes.

title: Strong vs eventual consistency
summary: Decide how fresh reads must be, knowing that stronger guarantees cost latency and availability.

values.strong: The latest committed write, as if there were one copy
values.eventual: Possibly stale data that converges if writes stop

values.strong: Higher: coordination across replicas on the critical path
values.eventual: Lower: answer from the nearest replica

values.strong: May reject requests to preserve correctness

values.eventual: The application must tolerate staleness and conflicts
Feeds, counters, caches, recommendations, search indexes

strong: A stale read could cause real harm or double spending.
You must enforce a uniqueness or balance invariant.
eventual: Slightly stale data is acceptable to the user.
You need low latency across regions or high availability.

watchOut: Mixing models silently: say per feature which one you provide.
Session guarantees such as read-your-writes often matter more to users than global ordering.
